MARKET.head: Bordeaux leads Liv-ex trade as Lynch-Bages 2005 becomes top-traded wine
MARKET.summ: US and UK buyers both upped their purchasing, the former segment reclaiming their share of purchasing
takeaways: Bordeaux held the lead with a 37.4% share of purchases on the Liv-ex trading platform this week.
Lynch-Bages 2005 was the top-traded wine overall, while Burgundy's share fell to 15.4% from 18.4%.
US buyers claimed over half of Bordeaux's purchased value, with their overall share rising to 9.6% from 7.0%.

MARKET.head: Surrey funds 17 rural projects, including a vineyard bird-repelling laser
MARKET.summ: A wine producer using bird-repelling lasers and cattle farmer using GPS collars to track livestock are among 17 innovative projects funded from a £500,000 pot to boost Surrey’s rural economy. Surrey County Council’s Farming Innovation Accelerator supports farmers and growers with funding for projects to modernise operations,...
takeaways: Surrey County Council's Farming Innovation Accelerator is funding 17 rural projects from a £500,000 pot.
Each recipient receives a grant of up to £35,000 plus bespoke expert support, drawn from UK Shared Prosperity Funding.
Albury Vineyard will install an automated bird-repellent laser to protect 18 acres of grapevines, adding over 1,700 bottles a year.

MARKET.head: Navarra rosé shows how demanding winemaking can become a premium selling point
MARKET.summ: How Navarra Rosado turned production challenges into premium positioning and a compelling marketing story. Andrea Ontiveros Flores, a sommelier and marketing & communications specialist from Alicante, Spain asks if English wine could do the same? Consumers rarely pay more simply because winemaking is difficult.
takeaways: Navarra rosado producers use the Saignée method, needing up to three times more grapes than standard red production.
The region's new Rosado Tradition designation requires Saignée and exclusive use of Garnacha to protect its premium positioning.

MARKET.head: Australian wine exports fall 7% as US losses outweigh Asian and Canadian gains
MARKET.summ:
Australian wine exports declined overall in the year ending September 2026, but the results varied significantly across markets. Strong growth in Southeast Asia and Canada was offset by more challenging conditions in the United States (US). 

This Market Bulletin will analyse the latest export data, released...
takeaways: Australian wine exports fell 7% in value to $2.25 billion in the 12 months to September 2026, with volume down 5%.
Exports to the US dropped 28% in value to $219 million, the biggest drag, while Canada rose 12% to $185 million.
Southeast Asia grew 16% in value to $291 million, led by Thailand's 57% rise to a record $73 million.

MARKET.head: Bordeaux leads fine wine trade at 39.6%, with Lafite 2005 top-traded
MARKET.summ: Bordeaux led the market, claiming 39.6%, Lafite accounting for over a quarter of its trade
takeaways: Bordeaux claimed 39.6% of traded value this week, with Lafite accounting for over a quarter of the region's value.
Burgundy fell to 18.4% from 24.8% last week, while Tuscany rose to 8.9% from 5.2%.
Bollinger overtook Dom Perignon and Louis Roeder as the top-traded producer by value, with R.D. 2008 the leading wine.

MARKET.head: VinePair weekly roundup covers SCOTUS home distilling case and Uncle Nearest sale
MARKET.summ: This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Diageo’s toxic chemical spill, SCOTUS to review a home distilling case, the latest product releases, and more.
takeaways: The Supreme Court agreed to review a case challenging home distilling restrictions.
Fawn Weaver moved to block a potential sale of Uncle Nearest, the whiskey brand she co-founded.
Mark Zuckerberg's Guinness publicity effort was reported as a flop, and Southern Glazer's faces a bribery snafu.

CULTURE.head: Ohio buyer uncovers 1930s-and-earlier wine and spirits cellar sealed since 1939
CULTURE.summ: John Smith had to actually buy the 10,600-square-foot stucco Tudor mansion before he would be able to open the wine cellar and find out what bottles had been left down there some 86 years earlier. Hidden off the main road at the end of a circular driveway, The Sherman Estates was built on fifteen acres of land in northwest...
takeaways: John Smith bought the 1925 Sherman Estate in Dayton, Ohio, and found its cellar sealed since John Q. Sherman died in 1939.
The roughly 400 bottles he found were all from the 1930s or earlier, including 1895 Niersteiner and 1934 Chanson sparkling Burgundy.
Smith sold one opened, half-full pre-Revolution Cuban Ron Bacardi bottle, dating to about 1919, to Bacardi's heritage curator for $1,000.

CULTURE.head: Plumpton College recruits Level 3 viticulture apprentices for November 9 cohort
CULTURE.summ: Develop the skills your business needs, invest in emerging talent and help shape the future of the UK wine industry with a Viticulture Apprenticeship at Plumpton College. As the UK wine industry continues to grow, developing a skilled workforce is essential to its long-term success. Plumpton College’s Level 3 Viticulture...
takeaways: Plumpton College is recruiting for its next Level 3 Viticulture Apprenticeship cohort, starting 9 November, with late joiners possibly accepted in January.
The apprenticeship combines workplace experience with college block weeks and is endorsed by WineGB and land-based sector bodies.
For eligible non-levy-paying SMEs, government funds 100% of training costs for apprentices aged 16 to 24, subject to funding rules.

CULTURE.head: Real Housewives shows reveal the sweet, mass-market wines their cast prefers
CULTURE.summ: What do the reality stars’ drinking habits reveal about wealth, taste, status and the economics of the U.S. wine industry?
takeaways: Cake Zine's essay, co-published here, argues Real Housewives cast members favour mass-market, high-alcohol, sweet wines, mostly Californian cabernet.
The author cites Mary Cosby's praise of 2003 Dom Pérignon, which she called the best because the heatwave made the grapes sweeter.
The essay links this taste to Robert Parker's 100-point system and 'Parkerization', which encouraged riper, fruit-forward wines.

SCIENCE.head: English vines hit by 2026 heatwaves; Bacchus struggled, Sauvignon Blanc thrived
SCIENCE.summ: With harvest complete, or nearing completion on many vineyards, Hutchinsons agronomists Rob Saunders and Will Robinson look at the impact of the record-breaking summer and what we can learn for future seasons. While 2026 could be remembered as a vintage season for some growers, others will look back less fondly, having first...
takeaways: Heatwaves in 2026 pushed 54 Met Office stations to all-time daily maximum records, peaking at 38.2°C in Gloucestershire in August.
Harvest ran 10-14 days earlier than normal, with Sauvignon Blanc showing high alcohol and phenolic ripeness while Bacchus struggled.
Viticulturist Markus Keller says photosynthesis stalls above 35°C, and brief extreme heat is worse than longer moderate heat.

SCIENCE.head: UK vineyards navigate early, hot, dry 2026 harvest after frost
SCIENCE.summ: After a run of dramatically different vintages, 2026 has given UK viticulture another season that challenged assumptions, but also demonstrated just how much English and Welsh vineyards can achieve. The 2026 growing season began with a series of extraordinary frost events, creating a challenging start before developing into a...
takeaways: 2026 began with a series of extraordinary frost events in UK vineyards before a warm, dry season developed.
Rapid ripening pushed harvest several weeks early at many English and Welsh vineyards, while dry weather kept disease pressure manageable.
Growers are now told to base picking decisions on fruit maturity monitoring rather than the calendar, as heat and drought become concerns.

SCIENCE.head: Domaine Bousquet details organic and water-saving practices at Mendoza winery
SCIENCE.summ: Domaine Bousquet continues to elevate Argentine wine through generations of dedication and innovation in organic wine practices. Earlier this year, Irma Remigio and her team warmly welcomed SWR’s Membership Manager, Ilva Fridenberga, to their winery. The winery, located at the foot of the Andes Mountains, is globally recognized...
takeaways: SWR Membership Manager Ilva Fridenberga visited Domaine Bousquet, a winery at the foot of the Andes in Mendoza, in February.
The winery is trialling biodiversity and garden vineyard corridors, harvesting from outside the vine rows in the biodiversity sections.
It switched to high-pressure hoses for cleaning harvest boxes after comparing water use, and is a signatory of the Bottle Weight Accord, targeting still bottles under 420g.

SCIENCE.head: MODIS satellite data validated for mapping vineyard water use in Italy
SCIENCE.summ: In North-Eastern Italy water demand for vineyards irrigation is constantly increasing, but this conflicts with the high civil and industrial rates of water consumptions in the area, which is one of the most densely populated in Europe
takeaways: Researchers at the University of Padova used MODIS satellite data to estimate evapotranspiration across a 25-hectare Italian vineyard.
Estimates were calibrated on two years of eddy-covariance measurements and independently validated on the other two years.
The results matched in situ observations well, suggesting MODIS can monitor vineyard evapotranspiration at regional scale.

SCIENCE.head: Portuguese trial cuts Loureiro and Borraçal yields with ethephon and thinning
SCIENCE.summ: Some years, climate conditions and biological events increment the fertility of vines, which can lead to over cropping and a decrease of wine quality
takeaways: A 2007 experiment in Vinhos Verdes vineyards tested chemical and manual methods to reduce yields of Loureiro and Borraçal vines.
Ethephon and manual bunch thinning significantly cut crop, with manual thinning reducing Borraçal yield by about 41% against control.
Ethephon at berries buck-shot size raised sugar and lowered acidity in Loureiro, while Borraçal gained no quality benefit.

SCIENCE.head: Grenache rootstocks and irrigation trials show lower water use under drought in Spain
SCIENCE.summ: Under the context of global change, any decrease in water use by crops is essential, because water is becoming a more and more scarce resource, especially in Mediterranean areas, where grapevines are grown
takeaways: Spanish researchers at IRTA-Torre Marimon grew three-year-old Grenache on rootstocks 110-R, 41-B and 161-49C, irrigated or non-irrigated.
Water use efficiency was higher in non-irrigated vines, and higher on 110-R and 41-B than on 161-49C.
Stomatal conductance stayed linked to leaf water potential in non-irrigated vines, but not in irrigated ones.

SCIENCE.head: Italian researchers outline viticulture strategies for climate, water and biodiversity challenges
SCIENCE.summ: In the globalization conditions possible future scenarios, optimistic and pessimistic are supposed
takeaways: Climate change may extend vineyard areas to higher altitudes and latitudes, requiring more stress-resistant grapevine genotypes.
Italian regions have launched projects to recover local grape varieties at risk of abandonment, preserving genetic biodiversity.
Researchers at the University of Pisa studied Malvasia of Lazio, Cesanese d'Affile and Cabernet Sauvignon under Conegliano cordon spur training.

SCIENCE.head: Conegliano pruning trials on Lazio grapes aim to raise saleable product value
SCIENCE.summ: In this work the salient results of the viticultural and ecomomic researches earned out on interesting italic varieties of Latium (Malvasia of the Lazio and Cesanese d'Affile) and an international vsriety (Cabernet sauvignon), "Cordon Spur of Conegliano" (CSC) as growing system, will be exposed
takeaways: Italian researchers from CRA, ARSIAL, and several universities tested the Cordon Spur of Conegliano growing system on Lazio varieties.
They compared Vertical Tridimensional Minimal Pruning of Conegliano with and without DMRC double maturation.
The stated aim is to raise Gross Saleable Product and exploit vineyard area for quality and originality.

SCIENCE.head: Winter vineyard jobs eased by pruning, soil and frost-protection tools
SCIENCE.summ: As autumn turns to winter a list of jobs looms large in the calendar. The vines need pruning and the soil needs care and attention. To make these jobs less demanding and costly, different tools can be used.
takeaways: Vineyard Magazine describes winter tasks including pruning and soil care, which tools can make less demanding and costly.
Zanon cordless battery secateurs are popular for hand pruning, and the Provitis tractor-mounted pre-pruner cuts time and effort further.
Late spring frost protection options include candles, wind machines and the Ventigel, which combines heat and wind.

SCIENCE.head: Vine balance concept and how it shifts over the growing season
SCIENCE.summ: Vine balance is a commonly used term in viticulture that expresses the concept of an appropriate balance of vegetative to reproductive growth of the vine
takeaways: Vine balance describes an appropriate balance between vegetative growth and reproductive growth in a grapevine.
A balanced vine has enough growth to ripen its crop, form fruitful buds for next year, and build reserves.
Common indirect measures such as yield-to-pruning-weight ratio do not capture how growth balances shift during the season.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Rabasco: beautiful natural wines from Abruzzo, Italy
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Rabasco is an impressive natural wine producer in Abruzzo, which is run by Iole Rabasco. She was previously
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Iole Rabasco, a former lawyer, runs the family estate Rabasco in Pianella, Pescara, Abruzzo, farming 11 hectares biodynamically since 2006.
Rabasco makes zero-sulfite, natural wines from vineyards over 40 years old, some aged in demijohns, with Iole owning 120 of them.
The author tasted the Rabasco range at the VinNatur tasting in Paris in November 2025, scoring the wines 93 to 94 out of 100.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A New White Zin
NEWSLETTERS.summ: If you are not familiar with the lore of White Zinfandel , America’s greatest contribution to wine culture , you are missing out on some excellent cocktail conversation. I understand this might sound like the layup for a bad wine joke, but I’m not being facetious. White Zinfandel is as important to the United States
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: Tim Atkin argues the US wine industry is due a successor to White Zinfandel, which he says still sold 49.2 million bottles in the US in 2024.
White Zinfandel originated with Bob Trinchero at Sutter Home, whose sweet, unintentionally off-dry rosé became a hit with American consumers from the 1980s.

Atkin proposes a new category called "Relevé": a field blend of red and white grapes from an entire estate or region, citing Will Marengo's Mrs. Crabtree's field blend from The Feudal Project as a model.

NEWSLETTERS.head: San Francisco’s Local-Wine Complex
NEWSLETTERS.summ: San Francisco and its immediate surrounds have never been more packed with places where a thirsty wine lover can sit
NEWSLETTERS.author: Alder Yarrow
takeaways: San Francisco and its surrounding area now host an unprecedented number of venues where wine drinkers can sit and drink.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A deeper look at underwater wine aging
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Is a wine from the depths ‘better’ or does it depend on the boat?
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: Attis, a winery owned by the Fariña family near O Grove, Galicia, ages its Albariño 'Mar' underwater in magnums in the estuary.
The 2025 Attis Albariño 'Mar' is aged five months underwater at 13-16C and is the same wine as its 'Standard' bottling, which makes about 120,000 bottles annually.
The author's experience of underwater-aged wines is that they generally taste more advanced in age and less fresh than landbound counterparts.

NEWSLETTERS.head: What to Know Before This Year’s Hospices de Beaune Wine Auction
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Discover the world's most famous charity wine auction held since 1859. Get essential tips and insights for this year's legendary Burgundy event
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jonathan Finch
takeaways: The 166th Hospices de Beaune wine sale takes place Sunday 15 November 2026, with the first lot due around 2.30pm.
Last year's sale raised €18.8 million, with Grand Crus averaging €86,290 a cask and Premier Crus €23,180.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Owendee
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The rituals of service for the holidays, plus this week’s favorite stories about food, wine, and culture
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Wine-related search queries slump in July but rise sharply through October, peaking on December 31, according to the author's search trend evidence.
The author notes the October-December wine-buying period coincides with the Northern Hemisphere harvest.
The author links the season's holidays, from Samhain and Halloween to Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year's, to the wheel of the year.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Visiting the Vineyard in the Sky
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The extraordinary story of Domaine de Beudon in Valais, Switzerland
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: Domaine de Beudon, a six-hectare Valais estate at 890 metres, is farmed by the Granges-Faiss family, reachable only by hiking or cable car.
Jacky Granges-Faiss bought the estate in 1971; Marion Granges-Faiss became Valais's first Demeter-certified estate in 1992.
Wines ferment at Beudon but are aged and bottled at Pierre-Antoine Crettenand's winery in Saillon, with sulphites the only additive since 2003.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Inside Chinon’s Lieux-Dits Project
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Vignerons lead a collective effort to recognize the vineyards behind the appellation’s Cabernet Francs
NEWSLETTERS.author: Cab Franc Chronicles
takeaways: Chinon's Syndicat launched a collective lieux-dits project in 2014 to promote vineyard sites without a formal classification or official hierarchy.
Seven lieux-dits have been officially recognized so far, starting with La Croix Boissée in Cravant-les-Côteaux in 2018.
Each recognized lieu-dit gets a detailed monograph and an engraved stone marker in the vineyard, and requires proposal by at least two vignerons.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Yet Another Vintage Port Flex Post (Tasting Selections From 1985 - 2022)
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Last week, I published a bunch of reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the (stellar) 2024 Port vintage. I typically follow those type of posts up with another post of other, older selections of vintage Ports that I tasted at the same event, and I offer them without much shame as simply […] This article was...
NEWSLETTERS.author: Joe Roberts
takeaways: 1WineDude published reviews of selections from the 2024 Port vintage after an NYC media tasting.
A follow-up post covers older vintage Ports tasted at the same event, spanning 1985 to 2022.

NEWSLETTERS.head: 400 Montepulciano Bottles for Thomas Jefferson circa 1805
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The wine everyone’s been gushing over since the middle ages!
NEWSLETTERS.author: Eveline Chartier
takeaways: A 1350 trade contract between the Del Pecora family and merchant Jacopo di Vanni of Santa Fiora is the oldest known document for Vino Nobile di Montepulciano.
Thomas Jefferson received 473 bottles of Montepulciano in November 1805 and requested 400 bottles annually, confined to crop from Jesuit vineyards.
A 2024 document unveiled by the Consorzio del Vino Nobile di Montepulciano dates the first known use of the term Vino Nobile to 1766 by the Jesuits.
